data.title: California Governor Gavin Newsom Signs Executive Order to Rein in AI Companies: NVDA, AAPL, GOOGL
data.description:
California Governor Gavin Newsom has signed an executive order aimed at addressing the potential dangers related to artificial intelligence (AI). The executive order is potentially consequential as many leading technology companies such as Nvidia (NVDA), Apple (AAPL), and Google parent company Alphabet (GOOGL) are headquartered in California's Silicon Valley.

Newsom is among the 2028 Democratic presidential candidates that are urging a more aggressive regulatory approach to rapidly evolving AI technologies, which has alarmed voters. But Congress appears unlikely to take any meaningful legislative action on AI fears right now and U.S. President Donald Trump has resisted calls for regulations, labeling the concerns a "hoax."

Gavin Newsom's Executive Order

"The federal government's abject failure to create any form of meaningful AI oversight or accountability should alarm every American, especially when AI CEOs themselves are begging for regulation," said Newsom in a news release. "We're not waiting to act – we're going to speed up our work on substantial and responsible AI oversight before it's too late."

Promotion

The California governor's executive order calls on a group of experts to meet and create, within two months, a guide for the state to strengthen its AI safety and security laws. Those enhanced laws may include a requirement for independent third parties to write safety plans for frontier AI companies, and/or mandate that companies develop a "kill switch" to shutdown their models in case of emergency.

Newsom, whose term as California governor ends on Jan. 4 of next year, has not formerly announced a presidential campaign, though he has said he is considering the possibility and political pundits expect him to run for the White House.

data.title: Boeing Stock (NYSE:BA) Ticks Up as Starliner Comes Back
data.description:
The Starliner program was a fairly big black eye to aerospace stock Boeing (BA). The debacle that followed, in which two astronauts were left on the International Space Station for around nine months instead of the original nine days it was expected to be, weighs on Boeing to this very day. But Starliner may be getting a new lease on life soon. This caught investors' interest, and Boeing stock ticked up fractionally in Friday afternoon's trading. Boeing has seen a 8.65% loss in its share price over the past year.

Winner By Default

Apparently, SpaceX (SPCX) is planning to wind down the Crew Dragon program. Given that the Crew Dragon saved the last Starliner mission and got Boeing's astronauts home safely, this leaves the whole space program without a reliable spacecraft. Thus, NASA is putting some extra work in to get the Starliner up and running, according to a report from Ars Technica.

NASA will be ordering another two crewed missions as early as next week, the report noted. Further, NASA will foot the bit for fixing the thruster issues and will even offer support to get launch duties squared away. SpaceX, the report noted, wants to focus on the Starship rocket and getting more Starlink satellites in orbit.

Lufthansa Steps Up Its Purchases

Boeing also landed some good news from The Lufthansa Group (DLAKY), who agreed to pick up more Boeing 737 MAX aircraft. Reports noted that Lufthansa had some additional options in reserve for purchase, and decided to exercise those options, picking up another 20 737 MAX 10 aircraft. The options came after Lufthansa agreed to pickup 40 737 MAX 8 aircraft back in 2023. The new MAX 10s, meanwhile, will not be delivered until the early 2030s.

data.title: Joby Aircraft Flies 3,199 Miles Across America With Zero Pilot Inputs
data.description:
Air taxi developer Joby Aviation (JOBY) has completed what it says was the first fully autonomous flight across the United States. Indeed, a converted Cessna Caravan equipped with Joby's technology traveled 3,199 miles from Concord, California, to North Carolina's Outer Banks with zero control inputs from the onboard safety pilot. The aircraft handled taxiing and takeoff on its own. It also navigated the route and completed its landings autonomously under remote supervision.

This is important because the flight tested the system in real-world conditions rather than on a short demonstration route.

During the trip, the aircraft crossed busy airspace and high-altitude terrain. It also adjusted its route around severe weather. Remote teams supervised the aircraft from Joby's California autonomy headquarters and Shaw Air Force Base in South Carolina. At one point, the flight was being supervised from as far as 2,323 miles away.

Promotion

Joby CEO JoeBen Bevirt said the journey offers a look at what autonomous aviation could eventually become.

Joby Is Building Autonomy for More Than Air Taxis

It is worth noting that the aircraft used for the trip was not Joby's electric air taxi. Instead, Joby installed its autonomous technology on a Cessna Caravan, which shows that the system could potentially work on different types of aircraft.

That creates opportunities outside passenger transportation. For example, Joby has suggested that autonomous cargo flights and emergency response could be potential use cases. The company is also testing defense logistics. Before the cross-country milestone, Joby said that the platform had already completed more than 400 flights and over 800 hours of automated flight time.

The stock initially moved higher after the announcement before giving up those gains. Joby shares remain down sharply this year as investors continue to weigh the large amount of spending needed to develop autonomous aircraft and the regulatory approvals required before fully autonomous commercial flights can become common.

data.title: "Largest Theft of Labor in Human History": Microsoft Stock (NASDAQ:MSFT) Dips as Ethical Implications of AI Training Creep In
data.description:
Tech giant Microsoft (MSFT) has a bit of an ethics problem right now, at least as far as its AI researchers are concerned. The researchers at OpenAI share similar concerns, noted a report from the New York Post. The researchers in question are starting to wonder if all the articles and such written by humans and fed into large language models (LLMs) might represent what one recently unsealed court document called the "…largest theft of labor in human history." The idea is a difficult one to parse, and investors shied away, sending Microsoft shares down fractionally in Friday afternoon's trading. Microsoft has posted a 3.9% loss in its share price over the past year.

Isn't That How Everyone Learns to Write, Though?

The documents described that large numbers of people would ultimately consider LLMs "…hoovering up…" written work to be "…an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions." Further, one OpenAI executive noted that its products would be an "existential threat" to publishers, ultimately. Yet Microsoft and OpenAI could defend their practices, saying that the articles that were taken were ultimately turned into new content, permissible by certain interpretations of copyright law like "fair use" principles.

This does make for a difficult issue, ethically. After all, people learn to write in much the same way. They read other people's written work, and learn to use these methods and principles in their own written work. Schools teach writing by reading. The question here ultimately becomes whether exposing an LLM to other people's work is theft, or just education. If it is theft, then what keeps every human writer from being branded a thief for doing much the same thing?

Microsoft may be having Blizzard start now, so that a new Diablo can be released as close to the series as possible, to take advantage of the interest.

data.title: Markets at Midday: U.S. Stocks Fall as 10-Year Treasury Yield Moves Back Above 5%
data.description:
U.S. equity markets are sliding lower at midday on Sept. 18 as the yield on the 10-year Treasury rises back above 5%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite indices are each in the red to end the trading week as spiking bond yields continue to pressure stocks. The 10-year Treasury yield was at 5.002% at noon hour, having risen from 4.966% earlier in the day.

The yield on the 2-year Treasury note rose more than five basis points to 4.743%, while the 30-year Treasury yield is up four basis points to trade at 5.336%. Yields on government bonds have steadily risen during the week as prices for U.S. Treasurys weaken. One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.

A Losing Week for U.S. Equities

The benchmark S&P 500 index is headed for a losing week, even after the index rebounded strongly on Sept. 17 following the Federal Reserve raising interest rates by 25 basis points, its first hike in three years. At noon on Friday, the S&P 500 is down 0.25%, while the Dow is down 0.48%, and the technology-laden Nasdaq (NDAQ) is trending 0.15% lower.

data.title: On Stock Rises After Kylian Mbappé Leaves Nike for Equity Deal
data.description:
Shares of Swiss sportswear company On Holding (ONON) are up in today's trading after signing football (soccer) star Kylian Mbappé, according to MT Newswires. The Real Madrid forward is leaving rival Nike (NKE) following a partnership that stretched back to his childhood. More importantly for On, the deal gives Mbappé an equity stake and makes him an important part of the company's push into soccer. Financial terms were not disclosed.

According to The Athletic, Mbappé agreed to join On after his Nike contract expired this summer. He also turned down more established football brands as On prepares to challenge companies that already dominate the shoe market.

Importantly, though, this is not a simple sponsorship where Mbappé wears On products. In fact, he will work directly with the company's product teams to help develop and test future football shoes and apparel.

data.title: Why Netflix Stock Is Down Today and Why There Could Be More "Downside Risk" From Here
data.description:
And down it goes again. Netflix (NASDAQ:NFLX) shares have been hammered over the past year amid a variety of concerns including slowing growth, weaker engagement, tougher competition, unease over its more ambitious M&A strategy and its content pipeline. And now the stock is being subjected to another beating in Friday's session.

The culprit appears to be the latest note from Wells Fargo analyst Steven Cahall, who has turned from skeptic to bear. Cahall has downgraded his NFLX rating from Equal Weight (i.e., Neutral) to Underweight (Sell) while also lowering his price target from $80 to $57, implying shares will shed 21% over the next year. (To watch Cahall's track record, click here)

The analyst believes engagement trends are becoming harder to ignore. Netflix averaged about 1.6 hours of viewing per subscriber per day in the first half of 2026, which Cahall estimates is 8% below the comparable period in 2023 after accounting for password-sharing changes and geographic mix. More importantly, he estimates viewing of Netflix's top 100 original titles declined 3% year over year. Those programs account for roughly 20% of total viewing and, in Cahall's view, are where much of Netflix's cultural relevance and member value comes from. He also points to Netflix's U.S. TV viewing share falling below 8%.

Cahall sees the streaming giant trying to compensate by broadening engagement. The platform is putting more emphasis on gaming, documentaries, reality programming and video podcasts, while its recommendation system appears to be encouraging viewers to explore a wider range of titles. The analyst sees an opportunity to turn Netflix into a broader entertainment hub, but argues that the company cannot afford to lose the blockbuster originals that generate the most attention.

Meanwhile, his analysis of more than 150 major titles leads him to expect a weaker second-half 2026 slate. Cahall estimates viewing of the top 100 Netflix originals will fall 21% year over year, while additional viewing from less prominent titles keeps total hours roughly flat. His base case calls for 96 billion viewing hours, compared with 101 billion in his bull case and 93 billion in his bear case. He also sees higher churn risk heading into 2027.

The analyst sees "tougher choices ahead." The company could ramp up content spending, although that would take time to produce results, license more third-party programming such as live sports from Fox or NBCUniversal, or pursue acquisitions. Any of these paths could make the Netflix story more complicated.

The analyst also acknowledges several ways his bearish thesis could prove wrong. Netflix is spending record amounts on content and has repeatedly delivered unexpected breakout hits. Its international slate is also difficult to forecast and could provide upside to his viewing estimates. Finally, Cahall notes that Netflix could retain more pricing power and deliver stronger margins than he currently expects.

Nevertheless, despite Netflix's forward P/E already having already fallen from around 30x to 21x, Cahall sees "more downside risk."

Cahall, however, is currently the Street's lone NFLX bear. Elsewhere, the stock claims an additional 25 Buys and 6 Holds, for a Strong Buy consensus view. At $95, the average price target points to 12-month returns of 32%. (See NFLX stock forecast)
